result: The authors developed a novel working memory task that dissociates past (encoded) and future (to-be-tested) locations of memory items. Twenty-five participants memorized two colored gratings presented in one axis and were tested in the orthogonal axis, with eye-tracking used to measure spatial biases in gaze during memory selection.
evaluation: The experimental design is clearly described (C4, C5, C12, C13) with appropriate sample size (C11, C65), proper eye-tracking methodology (C70, C71), and validated statistical approaches (C72). The orthogonal manipulation successfully dissociates past and future spatial attributes, enabling independent tracking of each component.

result: Participants successfully performed the dynamic working memory task with 70±2% accuracy and average reaction time of 1218±125 ms.
evaluation: Behavioral performance data (C14, C15) demonstrate that participants could perform the task above chance level, validating the experimental paradigm. The accuracy level indicates the task was appropriately challenging while remaining feasible.

result: After cue onset, saccades became biased toward the encoded (past) location of the selected memory item, starting around 200 ms post-cue, revealing that working memory retention continues to rely on past encoded locations even when items will be tested elsewhere.
evaluation: The past location bias is supported by significant cluster-based permutation tests (C17, p<0.001) with clear temporal onset (C18). This finding replicates prior work from the same lab (C49) and is well-supported by the eye-tracking data shown in Figure 1b.

result: Saccades also showed a bias toward the future (to-be-tested) location that emerged early after the cue, with past and future biases occurring at overlapping time windows. This represents the first demonstration of microsaccade bias to future-relevant memory locations.
evaluation: The future location bias is supported by significant statistical tests (C20, p<0.001) and temporal overlap analysis (C22). This is a novel finding (C50) demonstrated through the orthogonal manipulation, with clear evidence in Figure 1c-d showing concurrent consideration of both spatial attributes.

result: The gaze biases toward both past and future locations were driven predominantly by microsaccades and occurred similarly across different trial types (horizontal-to-vertical and vertical-to-horizontal).
evaluation: The microsaccade-driven nature of the effects is demonstrated in supplementary analyses (C23, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and the consistency across trial types (C24, Figure 1—figure supplement 3) rules out axis-specific confounds, strengthening the generalizability of the findings.

result: The past bias was relatively transient, while the future bias continued to increase in anticipation of the test stimulus and increasingly incorporated larger eye movements beyond the microsaccade range.
evaluation: The temporal dynamics are well-documented in extended time-range analyses (C25, C26, Figure 1—figure supplement 4), showing differential time courses for past and future biases. This suggests distinct functional roles for the two spatial representations.

result: Single-trial analysis of individual saccades revealed truly joint consideration of past and future memory attributes. Saccades biased toward the past location were predominantly also biased toward the future location, demonstrated by a significant interaction (F(1,24)=18.1, p<0.001, partial η²=0.43).
evaluation: The single-saccade analysis provides compelling evidence for joint consideration (C28-C34). The statistical interaction (C31) with follow-up tests (C32, C33) demonstrates that future bias occurs specifically for past-biased saccades. This bypasses the averaging problem (C27, C44, C45) and provides definitive single-trial evidence shown in Figure 2.

result: The study unveils that working memory simultaneously retains both past and future spatial attributes of memory contents, which are jointly accessed and reactivated during mnemonic selection, even at the single-trial level.
evaluation: This primary conclusion (C6, C7, C8, C35, C41) is well-supported by converging evidence from trial-averaged analyses, temporal overlap data, and critically, single-saccade analyses. The orthogonal experimental design enables clear dissociation and independent tracking of both attributes.

result: The data support the proposal that memory is fundamentally future-oriented while also demonstrating that past memory attributes are not forgotten even when they do not become relevant again.
evaluation: The findings provide evidence for both future orientation (C36) through the robust future bias, and retention of past attributes (C37) through the persistent past bias. This interpretation is supported by the experimental data and connects to theoretical frameworks in the literature.

result: The data argue against a simple remapping account where memory contents are directly transferred to future-relevant locations. No evidence for remapping was found in the period between encoding and cue.
evaluation: The remapping hypothesis is tested and rejected based on the presence of past location bias (C39) and complementary analysis showing no remapping during the delay period (C40, Figure 2—figure supplement 1). This strengthens the interpretation of simultaneous retention.

result: Microsaccades provide important methodological advantages for tracking spatial attention, including their discrete nature enabling single-trial analysis and their ability to track attention in any direction, not just left/right.
evaluation: The methodological advantages of microsaccades (C46-C48) are demonstrated through the current study's ability to track attention in orthogonal axes and at single-trial resolution. These claims are supported by citations and the successful application in the current paradigm.

result: The future location bias represents a content-specific memory attribute because the to-be-tested location was determined by the memory item's encoding location (not the cue color), and opposite locations were associated with the two memory items.
evaluation: The content-specificity argument (C52-C55) is logically sound based on the experimental design where cue color selected the item but the future location depended on encoding position (C53, C56, C57). This rules out non-specific anticipatory attention as the sole explanation.

result: The functional significance of retaining past locations (which were task-irrelevant) may involve helping individuate memory items or making memories more robust through multiple spatial frames, though the exact mechanism remains speculative.
evaluation: These claims (C58-C61, C64) are explicitly speculative interpretations. While the retention of past locations is empirically demonstrated, the functional reasons remain hypothetical. The authors appropriately acknowledge this uncertainty and suggest future experiments to test these possibilities.

result: The findings complement recent studies investigating working memory in dynamic contexts and parallel discoveries of joint consideration of allocentric and egocentric spatial frames.
evaluation: The contextualization within the broader literature (C62, C63) is appropriate and supported by relevant citations. The parallel to allocentric/egocentric frame findings strengthens the interpretation of multiple simultaneous spatial representations.

result: Working memory bridges past sensory information to future behavior and involves both past and future components, which are often conflated in conventional laboratory tasks but dissociated in dynamic real-world situations.
evaluation: These foundational claims (C1-C3, C9, C10) about working memory function and the limitations of conventional tasks are well-supported by established knowledge and appropriate citations. They provide sound motivation for the experimental approach.

result: While it is expected that future locations would be considered based on prior work on anticipatory attention, the joint retention and reactivation of both past and future attributes together is a novel and non-trivial finding.
evaluation: The claim distinguishes between expected findings (future consideration, C42) and the novel contribution (joint consideration, C43). This is supported by citations to prior work (C16) and clearly articulates the advance beyond existing knowledge.

result: Sample size was determined a priori based on previous similar studies, with three participants replaced due to chance-level performance to achieve the target of 25 participants.
evaluation: The sample size justification (C65) based on prior work is appropriate, and the replacement of poor performers (C66) is transparently reported. This represents sound methodological practice, though the a priori power calculation could have been more formally specified.
